scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Pukllay originated in the indigenous Yampara communities of Tarabuco, located in the Yamparáez province of Chuquisaca, roughly 65 kilometres from Sucre, Bolivia.
Its roots stretch into pre-Columbian agricultural and spiritual practices linked to the onset of seasonal rainfall and harvest cycles.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Pukllay is held at the start and climax of the rainy season, specifically during Christian Carnival and centrally on the second Sunday of March in Tarabuco, as well as at urban celebrations like the Carnival of Oruro and Entrada del Gran Poder.
Ritually, the dance invokes Tata Pujllay, an ambivalent entity embodying extreme fertility, risk, and vitality.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music for Pukllay is provided by ensembles playing various Andean duct flutes belonging to the pinquillo family.
The primary melody carrier is the senqatanqana (also termed toqoro or Senka Tenkana, meaning 'the growing nose'), a massive duct flute carved from thick reed with an external duct akin to the moceño.
Listen for the senqatanqana (toqoro), pinquillo, cherque (straight moceño), wajra (horn trumpet).

A deep, penetrating sonority defined by the reedy, hollow breath of oversized senqatanqana duct flutes and buzzing cherque flutes, counterpointed by the raw brassy drone of wajra horn trumpets. Beneath the winds, an uninterrupted percussive bed is created not by hand drums, but by the physical movements of dancers—heavy thumping wooden soles, high-pitched ringing bells from wide waist belts, and the dry metallic scrape of giant iron heel spurs.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Men dance costumed in representation of the Tata Pujllay, wearing a black leather montera shaped like a 16th-century Spanish conquistador helmet, adorned with flowers and pompons.

Their clothing includes a kunkaunku (small poncho), aymilla (shirt), calzuna (black trousers featuring broad white ruffles), sunri (multicolored knitted wool gaiters showing geometric motifs or llamas), and elevated wooden ujuta sandals carrying oversized iron spurs.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The core traditional expression belongs to the Yampara communities in the rural municipality of Tarabuco and wider Yamparáez province of Chuquisaca.
Developed from pre-Columbian ritual ceremonies of the Yampara ethnic group in the southern Andes of Bolivia, syncretised with Christian carnival calendars and colonial military parodies.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Pukllay is an indigenous Yampara ritual offering to ancestors, nature deities, and the ambivalent fertile spirit Tata Pujllay, centered on the construction of the sacred pucara altar. Outsiders should approach the ceremony with deep reverence, respecting sacred spaces, offerings, and communal protocols.

wardrobe.from_sources: Men dance costumed in representation of the Tata Pujllay, wearing a black leather montera shaped like a 16th-century Spanish conquistador helmet, adorned with flowers and pompons. Their clothing includes a kunkaunku (small poncho), aymilla (shirt), calzuna (black trousers featuring broad white ruffles), sunri (multicolored knitted wool gaiters showing geometric motifs or llamas), and elevated wooden ujuta sandals carrying oversized iron spurs. A broad tanned leather belt (sinchu) suspends small bells around the waist, accompanied by suspended purple scarves and white flags. Women wear a two-pointed decorative p'acha montera hat, an aymilla dress, an aqsu (finely woven skirt with animal and domestic motifs), and a lliklla shawl secured with a large silver pin. Setting centers on rural open spaces around the towering pucara altar, as well as formal carnival parades.

visual_brief.costume_notes: Men dance costumed in representation of the Tata Pujllay, wearing a black leather montera shaped like a 16th-century Spanish conquistador helmet, adorned with flowers and pompons. Their clothing includes a kunkaunku (small poncho), aymilla (shirt), calzuna (black trousers featuring broad white ruffles), sunri (multicolored knitted wool gaiters showing geometric motifs or llamas), and elevated wooden ujuta sandals carrying oversized iron spurs. A broad tanned leather belt (sinchu) suspends small bells around the waist, accompanied by suspended purple scarves and white flags. Women wear a two-pointed decorative p'acha montera hat, an aymilla dress, an aqsu (finely woven skirt with animal and domestic motifs), and a lliklla shawl secured with a large silver pin. visual_brief.setting_notes: Pukllay is held at the start and climax of the rainy season, specifically during Christian Carnival and centrally on the second Sunday of March in Tarabuco, as well as at urban celebrations like the Carnival of Oruro and Entrada del Gran Poder. Ritually, the dance invokes Tata Pujllay, an ambivalent entity embodying extreme fertility, risk, and vitality. It serves as an act of thanksgiving to ancestral spirits and nature deities for agricultural bounty and abundant crops, centered upon the pucara—a ladder-like timber altar draped in freshly harvested produce, green vegetation, and drinks. Socially and historically, it honours the fallen warriors of the 1816 Battle of Jumbate, uniting around 30,000 Yampara people across communal ayllus.
